title: Trump Administration orders CDC to change COVID-19 testing guidelines
description_short: Trump Administration orders CDC to change COVID-19 testing guidelines
description_medium: On August 25, 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention changed its COVID-19 guidance to discourage testing for people without symptoms, even after a known exposure. The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services directed the change, following Donald Trump’s calls to reduce testing. The shift came as schools were reopening and asymptomatic transmission remained a concern.
description_long:
On August 25, 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention revised its COVID-19 testing guidance. People without symptoms were advised not to get tested even if they knew they had been exposed to someone with the virus. The change narrowed the circumstances in which asymptomatic contacts were encouraged to test. The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services directed the revision after Donald Trump had repeatedly argued that the country should conduct fewer tests.

The guidance changed during a period when schools were attempting to reopen and outbreaks were being reported among students and staff. People without symptoms could still transmit the virus, so the new recommendation drew concern about missed infections among exposed contacts. The change concerned federal testing advice; it did not prevent states, clinicians, or individuals from testing people outside the recommended criteria. The available account gives no count of people who went untested and does not measure the effect on infections. It documents a consequential change in federal public-health guidance amid continuing transmission.

title: Trump: Two dead at Miami Deportation Center since Trump's inauguration
description_short: Trump: Two dead at Miami Deportation Center since Trump's inauguration
description_medium: Maksym Chernyak, a Ukrainian detainee at Miami’s Krome Service Processing Center, died after vomiting and having seizures. Hospital staff found bleeding in his brain and pronounced him brain dead. Reported on February 24, 2025, his death was the second at Krome since Donald Trump took office on January 20. Genry Donaldo Ruiz-Guillen, a Honduran detainee, had died there on January 23.
description_long:
Maksym Chernyak, a Ukrainian man held at Miami’s Krome Service Processing Center, began vomiting and having seizures before he was taken to a hospital. Medical staff found internal bleeding in his brain and pronounced him brain dead. His death was reported on February 24, 2025. He was the second detainee reported to have died at Krome since Donald Trump’s inauguration on January 20. Genry Donaldo Ruiz-Guillen, a Honduran man, died at the facility on January 23; ICE said he had experienced dizziness and epileptic seizures for months.

Reports about Krome also described detainees sleeping on floors and facing restrictions on phone calls. Those conditions were separate from the medical accounts of Chernyak’s and Ruiz-Guillen’s deaths, and the available information does not establish what caused either death or whether detention conditions contributed. Chernyak’s hospital finding identifies the brain bleeding but does not explain what led to it. The deaths brought attention to detainee health and medical care at the same facility within a little over a month, while leaving the circumstances and causes unresolved.

title: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_short: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_medium: On January 26, 2024, a federal jury ordered Donald Trump to pay writer E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million for defaming her. The award followed a 2023 verdict that found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation and awarded Carroll $5 million. The second jury considered Trump’s later denials and attacks on Carroll. Trump rejected the verdict and said he would appeal.
description_long:
A federal jury in New York ordered Donald Trump to pay E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million on January 26, 2024. The case concerned statements Trump made about Carroll after an earlier jury had found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation. That 2023 verdict resulted in a $5 million award. In the later trial, jurors considered whether Trump’s continued denials and attacks on Carroll’s credibility were defamatory and what damages they caused. They awarded Carroll $65 million in punitive damages and $18.3 million in compensatory damages.

The judgment was a civil defamation award, separate from the first case’s $5 million verdict. Judge Lewis Kaplan presided over the proceedings. Trump rejected the decision, said he would appeal, and continued to criticize Carroll publicly after the verdict. The jury’s award reflected its assessment of the harm caused by his post-verdict statements. This account describes the judgment at the time it was issued and does not state the eventual outcome of any appeal.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

title: Trump: Paul Manafort offers updates to Russian oligarch, US-banned Oleg Deripaska
description_short: Trump: Paul Manafort offers updates to Russian oligarch, US-banned Oleg Deripaska
description_medium: In July 2016, Paul Manafort, then Donald Trump’s acting campaign manager, emailed a contact in Russia with an offer to arrange private campaign briefings for Russian businessman Oleg Deripaska. The emails later became part of material obtained by Robert Mueller’s investigative team. Representatives for Manafort and Deripaska said the briefings never happened; the correspondence documents an offer, not a completed transfer of information.
description_long:
In July 2016, Paul Manafort, serving as Donald Trump’s acting campaign manager, emailed a contact in Russia and asked that a message be passed to Oleg Deripaska. Manafort wrote that private campaign briefings could be arranged if Deripaska wanted them. The exchange later appeared among Manafort’s emails obtained by Robert Mueller’s investigative team during its Russia investigation. Deripaska was a Russian business figure with longstanding ties to Manafort, including a failed investment and a disputed debt.

The email offered a wealthy Russian contact access to campaign information while Manafort was leading Trump’s campaign. Representatives for both men said the proposed briefings did not take place. The correspondence therefore establishes that Manafort made the offer, but it does not show that Deripaska received the briefings or that campaign information was transferred. The episode adds a documented contact to the account of Manafort’s business relationships and campaign role, while leaving the proposed exchange unrealized according to the representatives’ statements.

title: Trump: Corporations cut ties with Trump and the GOP after insurrection
description_short: Trump: Corporations cut ties with Trump and the GOP after insurrection
description_medium: After the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, companies announced limits on political donations to Republicans who opposed certifying Joe Biden’s victory. Dow said it would pause donations to the 147 lawmakers unless they were reelected; Marriott and others made similar pledges. Stripe stopped processing payments for Trump’s campaign site, and Shopify closed Trump-related stores. These decisions varied in scope and duration.
description_long:
In the days after the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, companies announced changes to political giving and business with Donald Trump or Republicans who challenged certification of Joe Biden’s victory. Dow said it would stop donations to the 147 Republican lawmakers who objected unless they were reelected. Marriott International, Morgan Stanley, and the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association made similar pledges. Coca-Cola, Verizon, AT&T, Comcast, and Facebook were among companies reported to be pausing political contributions.

Other companies acted directly on Trump’s business activity. Stripe said it would no longer process payments on his campaign website, while Shopify closed several Trump and MAGA online stores. Deutsche Bank decided against future business with Trump or his company after serving as a major lender, and Signature Bank closed two Trump accounts totaling more than $5 million. These were distinct responses: some paused donations, while others ended or restricted particular services or relationships. Together they showed corporate and financial institutions reacting to the attack and the lawmakers’ objections, without every company permanently severing every tie.

title: Trump: State Department fired oil-and-gas experts 7 months before Iran strikes
description_short: Trump: State Department fired oil-and-gas experts 7 months before Iran strikes
description_medium: The State Department dismissed analysts who modeled scenarios involving a possible closure of the Strait of Hormuz, including oil-and-gas specialists and an expert who tracked sanctioned tankers. The staffing cuts were described as reducing the department’s capacity to prepare for an Iran-related energy or security crisis. The available dates conflict, however, so the timing of the dismissals relative to later Iran strikes remains unresolved.
description_long:
The State Department dismissed analysts whose work included modeling a possible closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The affected staff reportedly included oil-and-gas specialists and an expert who tracked sanctioned oil tankers. Their work was connected to planning for energy and security disruptions involving Iran; the strait carries a substantial share of global oil shipments. The staffing reductions were described as leaving the department with less expertise for preparing for such a crisis.

The timing is unclear. The title places the firings seven months before the Iran strikes, while the synopsis dates them to June 2025 and the linked account refers to July layoffs alongside later strikes and a closure of the waterway. Those dates do not establish a consistent sequence. Until the event date and relationship to the strikes are reconciled, the personnel change and its claimed effect can be described, but not its precise timing. The record remains marked for context because this chronology affects the central claim.

title: Trump: NJ official accuses Trump of breaking the law to prevent competition
description_short: Trump: NJ official accuses Trump of breaking the law to prevent competition
description_medium: In April 1997, James Kennedy, head of New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, asked the state gaming regulator to investigate Donald Trump. Kennedy alleged that Trump violated a law protecting casino competition by trying to block an Atlantic City tunnel serving a developing casino district. State officials deferred the inquiry while Trump’s lawsuit over the project was pending; no investigation followed after the suit was dismissed.
description_long:
On April 22, 1997, James Kennedy, executive director of New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, asked the state Division of Gaming Enforcement to investigate Donald Trump. Kennedy alleged that Trump violated a state law intended to preserve competition among casinos by trying to stop a tunnel in Atlantic City. The proposed route would connect the Atlantic City Expressway more directly to the marina district, where hotels and casinos were being developed.

Trump had filed a federal lawsuit in February to block construction. He argued that Kennedy’s agency was funding projects beyond its constitutional remit and accused the state of helping his competitors. The New Jersey Attorney General’s office told the gaming authority not to investigate while the lawsuit was pending. After the case was dismissed, the state did not open an investigation into Kennedy’s allegation. Trump spent more than $500,000 fighting the tunnel by the end of July, according to the contemporaneous account. No state finding established that he broke the law.

title: Donald Trump announces 1776 Commission to end black history in schools
description_short: Donald Trump announces 1776 Commission to end black history in schools
description_medium: On September 17, 2020, Donald Trump announced an executive order creating the 1776 Commission, which he said would promote “patriotic” history in schools. He attacked the New York Times’ 1619 Project and critical race theory during a national debate over teaching slavery and racism. The announcement set out a federal effort to influence that debate; it did not itself change any school’s curriculum.
description_long:
Donald Trump announced an executive order creating the 1776 Commission on September 17, 2020. He presented it as an effort to promote “patriotic” history in schools and criticized the New York Times’ 1619 Project and critical race theory, which he said distorted the country’s history. His remarks came amid public disputes over how schools teach slavery, racism, and the nation’s past.

The proposed commission was a federal intervention in that debate, framed by Trump as a response to what he portrayed as an overly negative account of American history. The announcement drew criticism, including from commentator Ana Kasparian, who objected to the implication that students should learn less about racism and slavery. The action documented here is the executive order and Trump’s stated rationale. The announcement alone does not show that a particular school changed its instruction. The title’s claim that the initiative was intended to end Black history is an interpretation of its purpose, beyond the commission’s creation and the rhetoric used to promote it.

title: Trump: ICE kidnaps & tortures legal immigrant and father at Logan Airport
description_short: Trump: ICE kidnaps & tortures legal immigrant and father at Logan Airport
description_medium: ICE arrested Fabian Schmidt, a New Hampshire green-card holder, at Boston’s Logan Airport on March 7, 2025. His family said agents stripped him, forced him into a cold shower, questioned him while naked, kept him on the floor, and withheld food, water, sleep, and medication. They said he collapsed before receiving medical care. The alleged treatment was not independently confirmed, and physical assault was not established.
description_long:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Fabian Schmidt at Boston’s Logan Airport on March 7, 2025. Schmidt, a New Hampshire resident and green-card holder, was an electrical engineer and the father of an eight-year-old girl. His family said agents stripped him, forced him into a cold shower, questioned him while he was naked, and kept him on a mat on the floor. They also said he was denied food, water, sleep, and medication, and received medical care only after collapsing.

Schmidt was held at the Donald W. Wyatt detention facility in Rhode Island as of March 15. His family said agents demanded he surrender his green card. He had lived in the United States since 2008 and had no criminal record beyond a decade-old DUI. The treatment allegations came from his family, and the available account does not independently confirm each detail. It also does not establish that he was physically assaulted. The incident centers on his arrest and detention and on serious claims about his treatment in custody, whose full circumstances remained unresolved.

title: Trump: In Russia, Donald Trump meets son of Mogilevich's NYC underboss
description_short: Trump: In Russia, Donald Trump meets son of Mogilevich's NYC underboss
description_medium: Donald Trump traveled to Moscow with Howard Lorber during the first week of November 1996 to explore land and trademark opportunities for a possible development. The timeline says Trump met Felix Sater there; Sater’s father, Mikhail Sheferovsky, was identified as an associate of Semion Mogilevich. The Russian projects were never built. Trump later worked with Sater’s Bayrock Group on Trump SoHo, while Lorber advised his 2016 campaign.
description_long:
Donald Trump traveled to Moscow during the first week of November 1996 with businessman Howard Lorber to explore land and trademark opportunities for a possible Russian development. The timeline says Trump met Felix Sater during the trip. It describes Sater as a Russian-American businessman who had fled to Russia while facing U.S. charges, and identifies his father, Mikhail Sheferovsky, as a New York underboss for Semion Mogilevich. These descriptions concern Sater and his family; they do not establish wrongdoing by Trump.

Trump later said the trip led to discussions with Moscow’s local government, but the properties were never built. The visit preceded later connections in Trump’s business and political circles: Trump partnered with Sater’s Bayrock Group on Trump SoHo, and Lorber became an adviser to Trump’s 2016 campaign. The account links the Moscow trip to those later relationships but does not show that it produced a completed Russian development. Its documented focus is Trump’s visit and the business contacts associated with it.
